strengths: Introduces a unifying conceptual lens—the effective noise scale—that connects several previously separately-studied optimizer/data hyperparameters (learning rate, weight decay, batch size, augmentation) to model merging compatibility, which is a novel angle beyond prior work linking noise only to single-model flatness/generalization.

Very broad empirical validation: multiple architectures (MLP, ResNet, DenseNet, Transformer/GPT, CLIP ViT, ConvNext), multiple datasets/tasks (SVHN, CIFAR10/100, TinyImageNet, WILDS-FMoW, RESISC45, TinyStories), and multiple merging paradigms (linear interpolation and task arithmetic), plus transfer learning settings, lending reasonably good external validity to the qualitative trend.

The identification of a non-monotonic 'sweet spot' in noise scale for merging effectiveness is an interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive finding, with reasonable supporting evidence (Figure 1, Figures 15-16 showing failure at extremes).

Good use of appendix materials providing extensive additional plots (per-dataset breakdowns, loss landscape slices, Hessian sharpness, hill-to-valley transition analysis) that support the narrative and improve reproducibility/transparency.
Practical relevance: findings could inform practitioners on how to tune training recipes to improve downstream mergeability, an actionable and underexplored question.
weaknesses: The 'unifying' claim for the effective noise scale is only explicitly demonstrated via reparameterization in one controlled experiment (Figure 1, learning rate x batch size on CIFAR100/ResNet18); the individual factor ablations (Sections 3.2-3.4) do not re-derive or verify the unified S̃ curve, so the paper mostly shows that each factor individually exhibits a qualitatively similar (not quantitatively unified) trend rather than rigorously validating one scalar quantity across all axes simultaneously (e.g., weight decay, augmentation).

No new theory is developed; the effective noise scale formula is adopted from prior SDE-based analyses (Mandt et al., Smith et al., McCandlish et al.) without new derivations specific to the merging/global landscape setting, making the core theoretical contribution thin relative to the empirical claims.

The explanation for weight decay's effect relies on the 'effective learning rate' argument, which is only shown to hold for scale-invariant architectures; the negative result for MLP/SVHN, while acknowledged, somewhat weakens the generality of the unifying framework as a single scalar across all architectures.

Much of the evidence is correlational: the paper documents that noise-related hyperparameters correlate with merging gains, but does not fully disentangle confounds such as different single-model capacity/feature-learning trajectories, or possible implicit changes in effective batch statistics, weakening claims of a causal, mechanistic link.

Task arithmetic experiments (Section 4) are less systematic than the linear interpolation experiments—fewer datasets, less rigorous connection back to the effective noise scale metric, and the results (e.g., initialization-dependent dichotomy) are presented more anecdotally without a unifying quantitative story.

No experiments at a scale resembling state-of-the-art LLMs/vision foundation models used in real merging applications (largest model is a 2-layer GPT and CLIP ViT-B/16 fine-tuning); the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this, which limits significance for practitioners merging large modern models.

Statistical rigor is somewhat limited: most conclusions rest on violin/scatter plots without explicit significance testing across seeds, and 'sweet spot' locations are not consistently characterized quantitatively across settings (e.g., no attempt to predict the optimal noise scale value a priori).

strengths: Extensive empirical sweeps across many architectures (MLP, ResNet, DenseNet, Transformer/GPT), datasets (SVHN, CIFAR10/100, TinyImageNet, WILDS-FMoW, RESISC45, TinyStories), and settings (from-scratch training, transfer learning, linear interpolation and task arithmetic), which gives the claims broad empirical coverage.

The attempt to unify several disparate optimizer knobs (learning rate, weight decay, batch size, augmentation) under a single 'effective noise scale' is a conceptually appealing framing that connects to existing SDE-based views of SGD.

Good appendix documentation of training/merging protocols and numerous supplementary figures (failure cases with too-large LR/WD, loss landscape slices, sharpness measurements, transition-phase hill-to-valley plots) that support reproducibility of the specific experimental choices made.
Identification of the dichotomy between pretrained and from-scratch initialization in task-arithmetic merging (Section 4.1) is an interesting and non-obvious empirical observation.
weaknesses: The central 'unifying' claim rests on a single alignment plot (Fig. 1, ResNet18/CIFAR100 only); the normalized proxy S̃ = η/(B(1-μ)^2) is a known quantity from prior SDE-noise-scale literature (Mandt et al. 2017; McCandlish et al. 2018) and is not actually used to quantitatively predict where the 'sweet spot' lies in other settings—it is only used qualitatively/post-hoc to re-explain already-observed trends in LR, WD, batch size, and augmentation separately, which weakens the claim that it is a truly unifying, predictive quantity.

No theoretical model or mechanism is provided for why a non-monotonic 'sweet spot' should exist, nor any quantitative formula for predicting its location given architecture/dataset; the contribution is descriptive curve-matching rather than a tested predictive theory, despite the title's framing as explaining 'how' the optimizer biases the landscape.

Data augmentation and weight decay are discussed as increasing the 'effective noise' qualitatively, but the covariance term Σ_A in Eq. 3 that is supposed to capture augmentation/data-diversity effects is never estimated or incorporated quantitatively into the proxy S̃ actually used in experiments—so the augmentation and weight-decay results are not actually unified under the same measured quantity as the LR/batch-size results, undermining the core unification claim.

Reported merging gains are often very small (e.g., 0.2-1.2 percentage points) with substantial overlap in the violin plots (Figs. 2,3,4), and no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals across more than a handful of seeds is reported, making it hard to assess whether the trends are robust versus noise, especially given only 2-3 seeds in several transfer-learning experiments.

Merging effectiveness is evaluated at a fixed α=0.5 for linear interpolation rather than optimizing/reporting over the full interpolation curve, which could confound 'gain' comparisons for solutions with different single-model accuracies or landscape curvatures.

The task arithmetic results (Section 4) show behavior that depends heavily on initialization in ways that seem to contradict the simple 'more noise = more compatible up to a point' narrative built in Section 3, and the paper does not reconcile or theoretically unify these dichotomous findings beyond describing them.

Overall contribution is largely incremental: it extends well-established single-model observations (large LR/large WD/small batch/augmentation induce flatter minima and better generalization) to merging compatibility without providing new algorithms, theoretical guarantees, or an actionable method practitioners could use beyond 'try moderately aggressive hyperparameters,' which is already common practice.

The paper explicitly acknowledges no theoretical guarantees and no large-scale experiments, and the real-world significance of the findings for state-of-the-art merging pipelines (e.g., merging large LLMs or billion-parameter vision models) remains unverified.

strengths: Identifies a unifying quantity, the effective noise scale, that consolidates the effects of learning rate, weight decay, batch size, and data augmentation on model merging success, providing a more parsimonious explanation than treating each hyperparameter separately.

Extensive empirical validation across diverse architectures (MLP, ResNet, DenseNet, Transformer/GPT) and datasets/tasks (SVHN, CIFAR10/100, TinyImageNet, WILDS-FMoW, TinyStories, RESISC45), as well as settings (training from scratch, transfer learning, task arithmetic).

The non-monotonic 'sweet spot' finding for merging effectiveness as a function of effective noise is an interesting and somewhat counterintuitive result, moving beyond prior work connecting noise mostly to flatness/generalization of individual minima to the global landscape and cross-solution compatibility.

Good coverage of ablations (learning rate, weight decay via effective learning rate framing, batch size, augmentation) with consistent qualitative trends reported, plus failure cases (too high noise) explicitly documented in appendix, improving the honesty/completeness of the empirical story.
Investigates both linear interpolation and task arithmetic merging, and shows interesting asymmetries depending on initialization (pretrained vs. from scratch), which is a nontrivial nuance.
Reasonably detailed experimental setup described in appendix (training/merging procedures, hyperparameters), aiding reproducibility to some extent.
weaknesses: The work is purely empirical/correlational; no formal theoretical derivation connects the proposed effective noise scale proxy to actual merging loss landscape geometry (e.g., barrier height, basin alignment) beyond intuitive SDE arguments borrowed from single-model literature. The causal mechanism for why noise affects cross-solution compatibility remains largely hand-wavy.

The effective noise scale normalization used in practice (S_tilde = eta / (B(1-mu)^2)) omits the gradient-noise covariance trace term from Eq. 3 in most experiments; augmentation and architecture-dependent noise are treated qualitatively rather than merged quantitatively into one scale, slightly overstating the 'unifying' claim.

Most central experiments (Figures 1-4) use a single architecture/dataset (ResNet18/CIFAR100) for the core unifying claim, with other datasets/architectures relegated to appendix without the same thorough joint sweep of batch size and learning rate.

The 'sweet spot' location is not characterized quantitatively (no fitted functional form, no prediction of where the optimum lies for a new setting), limiting the predictive utility of the claimed unifying law beyond qualitative trend-matching.
Weight decay results are explicitly inconsistent for non-scale-invariant architectures (MLP/SVHN), somewhat weakening the generality of the 'weight decay = noise' framing as a universal mechanism.

Reported gains are often small in absolute magnitude (e.g., 0.2-1.5% accuracy gains) and statistical significance/variance across seeds is shown via violin plots/scatter but not formally tested, raising questions about robustness of some comparisons.

The task arithmetic section is comparatively thinner and more descriptive, with less systematic decomposition of noise components (only learning rate studied) compared to the linear interpolation section.

No operationalization of the findings into an improved merging method or concrete hyperparameter selection recipe; the contribution is primarily explanatory/diagnostic despite the abstract's suggestion of leveraging training dynamics to improve merging.

Limited engagement with very recent large-scale merging studies (e.g., task arithmetic at scale); it remains unclear whether the findings generalize to the large-model regime most practitioners care about.

strengths: Addresses an important, underexplored question: why do optimization dynamics determine whether independently trained models can be successfully merged, going beyond prior work that only links noise to single-model flatness/generalization.

Very extensive empirical evaluation across many axes: architectures (MLP, ResNet18, DenseNet121, ViT, ConvNext, GPT-2/Transformer), datasets (SVHN, CIFAR10/100, TinyImageNet, TinyStories, WILDS-FMoW, RESISC45), merging methods (linear interpolation, task arithmetic, TIES, SWA), and optimizer components (learning rate, weight decay, batch size, momentum, augmentation, optimizer choice, scheduler).

The 'effective noise scale' offers an intuitive unifying lens that consolidates several previously disparate observations (large LR, small batch, momentum, weight decay via effective LR) into one quantity, and the paper demonstrates a consistent non-monotonic relationship with merging gain across settings.

Goes beyond simple accuracy-gain plots to connect findings to mechanistic explanations: permutation symmetry/rebasin ease, feature (CKA) alignment/diversity, Hessian-based sharpness, and 2D loss-landscape slices, adding some depth to the causal story.
Very thorough appendix with many additional experiments (schedulers, optimizers, transfer settings, TIES with 3 tasks, SWA interactions) that substantially strengthen robustness of the core claims.
Practical implication is useful and actionable: practitioners could potentially reduce hyperparameter search dimensionality by focusing on effective noise level rather than each component separately.
weaknesses: The work is purely empirical/correlational; no theoretical derivation or model explains why the noise-mergeability curve is non-monotonic or predicts the location of the 'critical point,' which the authors acknowledge as a limitation but which limits the depth and generality of the contribution.

The effective noise scale S̃ is a heuristic proxy (assuming tr Σ_A constant across runs) rather than a rigorously validated unifying quantity; the paper mostly shows qualitative alignment of curves (Figure 1) rather than quantitative goodness-of-fit or predictive power across settings.

The task-arithmetic results (Section 4) show a clear dichotomy — larger LR helps mergeability under transfer-learning initialization but hurts it under non-transfer initialization — which complicates and partially undercuts the paper's central unifying narrative that noise straightforwardly governs merging success.

Models studied are relatively small-scale (ResNet18/DenseNet121, 2-layer GPT, ViT-B/16 CLIP), and the paper explicitly states no large-scale experiments were run, despite motivating the problem with references to frontier-scale merging (e.g., Command A); it remains unclear how well the findings transfer to modern LLM/large-scale merging pipelines.

Merging-effectiveness metrics vary across sections (accuracy gain, loss gain, normalized accuracy), and it is not always clear how comparable conclusions are across these different measures, or how sensitive results are to the specific bifurcation/decay training protocol (WSD checkpoints) used throughout.

Statistical reporting is somewhat inconsistent — while violin plots suggest many points, it is unclear how many are truly independent training runs versus checkpoints from a shared stable-phase trajectory (partially correlated samples), and formal significance testing or confidence intervals for the core claims (e.g., critical point location) are largely absent.

The core individual findings (large LR/small batch/high momentum yields flatter minima and links to generalization) are largely consistent with well-established prior literature; the main novel contribution is the merging-specific reframing and the noise-scale unification, which, while useful, is somewhat incremental in conceptual novelty.

strengths: Very extensive empirical study spanning multiple architectures (MLP, ResNet18, DenseNet121, GPT, CLIP ViT, ConvNext), datasets (SVHN, CIFAR10/100, TinyImageNet, TinyStories, WILDS-FMoW, RESISC45), and merging schemes (linear interpolation, task arithmetic, TIES, SWA, permutation/re-basin).

The attempt to unify disparate optimizer hyperparameters (learning rate, weight decay via effective learning rate, batch size, momentum, augmentation) under a single 'effective noise scale' proxy is a reasonable and intuitive organizing idea, and the paper performs many ablations to probe it.
Good supplementary analyses connecting noise to feature alignment (CKA) and to permutation/re-basin compatibility, offering a more mechanistic story than accuracy numbers alone.
Reasonably transparent about limitations (no theory, limited scale) and discloses LLM assistance for writing.
weaknesses: The 'effective noise scale' is not actually validated as a unifying causal quantity; it is a heuristic proportionality (Eq. 3) that assumes tr Σ_A(θ_t) is roughly constant across runs, yet several reported manipulations (e.g., turning augmentation on/off) directly change Σ_A, so the proxy S̃ is being used outside its stated regime of applicability without quantitative verification that it tracks the true noise magnitude.

The core claim of a single non-monotonic 'critical point' governing merging success is contradicted by the paper's own task-arithmetic results: for non-transfer learning, larger LR yields *sharper* minima (opposite trend to linear interpolation and to the transfer-learning TA case), which is explained away post hoc via 'importance of initialization' rather than being predicted by the unifying theory. This undermines the central unifying narrative.

No theoretical derivation or model connects effective noise to the global loss-landscape geometry between independently trained solutions; the contribution is almost entirely descriptive/correlational curve-fitting across many hyperparameter sweeps, with the 'critical point' identified post hoc for each setting rather than predicted a priori.

Limited scale and generality: experiments use small/medium models (ResNet18, DenseNet121, 2-layer/6-layer toy Transformers, CLIP ViT-B/16) and the paper explicitly acknowledges no large-scale validation, raising concerns about whether the observed trends hold for the large foundation models where merging is actually deployed in practice (e.g., Cohere, LLM merging at scale, as cited in the intro).

The practical takeaway is weak: the paper does not propose an algorithm or actionable method to exploit the effective-noise finding (e.g., an adaptive noise-scheduling procedure for mergeable training), limiting its usefulness beyond a post hoc explanatory narrative; the conclusion even states 'many open questions remain' without concrete next steps.

Effect sizes in many figures are small (often <1-2% accuracy gain) with visible overlap in violin plots/scatter, and statistical significance across seeds is not rigorously quantified (mostly 1-3 seeds in several settings), weakening confidence in the fine-grained non-monotonic trend versus noise.

The decomposition into individual optimizer components substantially overlaps with well-established prior findings (Keskar et al. 2016; Jastrzebski et al. 2017; Smith et al. 2018; Van Laarhoven 2017) on noise/flatness of single minima; the paper's novelty is primarily in re-purposing these known relationships for the merging setting, which is a narrower, incremental extension rather than a fundamentally new mechanistic insight.

The task-arithmetic and TIES experiments (Section 4) reveal that optimal noise for individual merging compatibility conflicts with optimal noise for best absolute merged performance (Fig. 8), and conversely good mergeability across different hyperparameters is lost precisely when noise is tuned for best performance — this tension is noted but not resolved or theoretically explained, leaving the practical guidance muddled.

strengths: Unifying conceptual framing: the effective noise scale offers a parsimonious explanation that collapses multiple independent optimizer knobs (lr, batch size, momentum, weight decay, augmentation) into a single predictive quantity for merging outcomes, which is a genuinely useful simplification for practitioners and researchers.

Extremely thorough and systematic empirical validation: experiments span multiple architectures (MLP, ResNet18, DenseNet121, ViT, ConvNext-T, GPT-2), datasets (SVHN, CIFAR10/100, TinyImageNet, WILDS-FMoW, RESISC45, TinyStories, WikiText-103), and merging methods (linear interpolation, task arithmetic, TIES, SWA), with a large appendix of robustness checks.

The non-monotonic 'critical point' finding is a nontrivial and somewhat surprising result that goes beyond naive 'more noise = flatter = better' intuitions prevalent in prior literature, and is consistently replicated across settings.

Good decomposition studies isolating each optimizer component (Section 3.2-3.4) while controlling for single-model accuracy, which strengthens the causal story (i.e., ruling out that gains are simply due to better single-model performance).

The connection to permutation symmetry and feature alignment (Section 5) adds a plausible representational-level mechanism, linking noise-induced feature diversity to merge compatibility, which deepens the analysis beyond pure correlation.
Clear, well-organized writing with appropriate contextualization relative to prior work on linear mode connectivity, SGD noise theory, and weight decay's role in scale-invariant networks.
Honest and specific limitations section acknowledging the lack of theory and large-scale experiments.
weaknesses: The work is purely empirical/correlational; no theoretical model or mechanism is derived to explain why intermediate noise produces maximal mergeability beyond qualitative appeals to flatness and feature diversity, which limits predictive/generalizable value.

The effective noise scale formula (Eq. 3) treats tr Σ_A(θt) as roughly constant within a fixed augmentation regime, but this is a strong simplification; the paper does not rigorously validate how well S̃ alone (ignoring the data/gradient covariance term) predicts the critical point location across very different architectures/datasets, nor provide quantitative correlation metrics for this core claim beyond visual alignment of curves in Figure 1.

Experiments are restricted to relatively small-scale models/datasets (ResNet18/DenseNet121 on CIFAR/TinyImageNet, small 2-layer GPT, ViT-B/16 finetuning); given the paper explicitly motivates itself via application to 'state-of-the-art architectures,' the absence of larger-scale LLM or billion-parameter model validation is a meaningful gap that limits claims of broad significance.

The 'critical point' itself is not characterized quantitatively (e.g., no formula or scaling law predicting its location as a function of architecture/dataset/task), so the practical actionability of the finding (how to choose hyperparameters to hit this optimum) remains vague beyond 'try moderately larger noise.'

Some results are presented with limited statistical rigor (e.g., few seeds in several plots, no significance testing on the accuracy gain differences), making it hard to assess whether some observed trends (e.g., the TIES vs TA differences, momentum effects) are robust versus noise in the merging evaluation itself.

The task arithmetic section (Section 4) reveals an apparent dichotomy (larger lr good for transfer learning init, bad for non-transfer learning init) that is explained post-hoc but not predicted by the effective noise framework, somewhat undercutting the claimed unifying power of the main thesis.

Related work on model merging at scale and compute-optimal considerations could be more deeply engaged, and the discussion of how these findings might transfer to production-scale merging pipelines (e.g., Command A, LLM merging) remains speculative.
